title: Build synthetic reference image test fixture
description: Create `tests/images.py` producing deterministic synthetic RGB images with a wide, well-populated L* distribution and real chroma. The round-trip test's difficulty depends entirely on this fixture: a flat or narrow-histogram image would make the match trivially easy and hide real bugs, so the generator must fill most of the L* range and include saturated colors that stress the gamut-clipping path.
acceptanceCriteria: `synthetic_reference(rng, height=128, width=192) -> np.ndarray` returns uint8 (H, W, 3)
The same seed produces a byte-identical image (determinism)
The image's L* histogram at 256 bins has at least 200 non-empty bins, proving a broad distribution
The image contains saturated colors: at least some pixels have Lab chroma `sqrt(a*^2 + b*^2) > 40`
The image is not a flat gradient only — it includes distinct colored regions and mild noise
`flat_image(value, height, width) -> np.ndarray` produces a single-color image for the degenerate edge-case tests
`gradient_image(height, width) -> np.ndarray` produces a smooth grayscale ramp for the banding test
A self-test asserts every property above; `ruff check` clean

steps.details: Import numpy and the project's `srgb_to_lab` and `l_histogram` (used by the self-test). All generators take an explicit `rng` where randomness is involved so results are reproducible.

Create a 2-D diagonal luminance ramp with `np.linspace` over both axes combined (e.g. `(x_ramp[None, :] + y_ramp[:, None]) / 2`) scaled to the full 0-255 range. Broadcast to three channels. This guarantees broad L* coverage before anything else is added.

Stamp several rectangular patches with strongly saturated colors (pure red, green, blue, cyan, magenta, yellow, plus a couple of random saturated RGB triplets from `rng`). Place them at deterministic positions computed from the image size so the layout scales with H and W. These are what exercise the gamut-clipping path in TASK-5.

Add `rng.normal(0, 4, size=shape)` and clip to [0, 255] before casting to uint8. The noise fills in histogram bins that a pure gradient would leave sparsely populated, which is what makes the >=200-non-empty-bins criterion achievable.

Write `flat_image(value, height=32, width=32)` returning `np.full((h, w, 3), value, dtype=np.uint8)` for degenerate tests, and `gradient_image(height=64, width=1024)` returning a smooth grayscale ramp (identical across channels) for the anti-banding check.

Create `tests/test_images.py`: (a) determinism — two calls with the same seed are `np.array_equal`; (b) shape and dtype; (c) convert to Lab, histogram L* at 256 bins, assert `np.count_nonzero(counts) >= 200`; (d) assert `l.min() <= 5` and `l.max() >= 95`; (e) assert `np.max(np.hypot(lab[...,1], lab[...,2])) > 40`; (f) `flat_image(128)` has exactly one unique value; (g) `gradient_image()` has more than 200 unique grey levels.
Run `.venv/bin/pytest tests/ -q` and `.venv/bin/ruff check src tests`. If the non-empty-bin count falls short, increase the noise sigma or the gradient's span rather than lowering the threshold.

technicalNotes: The >=200-non-empty-bins assertion is a guard on the fixture's quality, not on the product. If it ever starts failing, the fixture got weaker and the round-trip test silently got easier — fix the fixture.
Keep the image small (128x192 default) so the full 6-seed round-trip suite stays fast; that is still ~25k pixels, plenty to populate 256 bins.
Saturated patches are deliberately included so `clipped_fraction` is sometimes non-zero in the pipeline tests, exercising a code path that a pure grayscale fixture would never reach.
Do not seed from the global numpy random state; every generator takes `rng` explicitly.
